entry.title: The 6 Very Best Dashcams
entry.summary: Get that collision on camera, whether on the road or while you’re parked.
entry.content:
If you’re ever unfortunate enough to be involved in a car accident, you’ll likely have to deal with insurance claims and lawyers. A dashcam (which mounts directly to your car’s dashboard or rearview mirror, or comes preinstalled on some newer cars) can help build your case. “The more information you have when dealing with a motor vehicle accident, it certainly supports a pursuit of the truth, because if a picture’s worth a thousand words, a motion picture is probably worth a million words,” says Jarod Krissman, an attorney at Krissman & Silver LLP in Long Beach, California. If you’re injured in an accident and have footage of the crash, he says, that footage can be evidence to determine who’s at fault. “It’s also there as a way for people who are mistakenly but wrongfully accused of negligence to prove the fact that they weren’t negligent,” he adds.

That’s the best kind of evidence to show your insurer in the event of a collision, says Robert Passmore, department vice president of personal lines at the American Property Casualty Insurance Association, who spent two decades handling claims at a national insurer before joining the trade group. A small but significant share of collisions wind up in a dispute, and video can help end the argument by showing what actually happened. “It doesn’t have a viewpoint, just like the damage to the vehicle doesn’t have a viewpoint,” Passmore says. “The video gives the unvarnished truth.”

To find the best dashcams, I interviewed seven experts — mobile electronics installers, a camera retailer’s senior technologist, two independent reviewers, an insurance-industry claims veteran, and the marketing director of a specialist dashcam retailer — and checked their picks against manufacturers’ spec sheets and manuals, keeping in mind a car that sleeps in a garage, one that survives alternate-side parking on a Brooklyn street, and the one your teenager drives to college each needs something different.

You’ll find single (front-only), dual (front and rear), and three-channel (with an interior cabin camera or an extra telephoto lens) on the market. So which to choose?

“A front-only camera is still worth having,” says Joseph Choi, director of marketing and new business at BlackboxMyCar, a specialist dashcam retailer. “It captures the most common evidence in front of the vehicle and is the simplest, least expensive way to get protected.”

A two-camera configuration, however, is considered the minimum by most of our experts. If you only have a front-facing camera, you won’t have any evidence if you get rear-ended. “I’ve gotten just as much use out of the rear cam as I do the front,” says Ariel Bravy, founder of independent review site Vortex Radar. Mark Steinberg, senior technologist at B&H Photo Video, sees the same thing at the register. “I think many people who buy them with just a front camera will come back” for the rear unit later, he says.

While a third, cabin-facing camera sounds like something for Uber drivers who need visual evidence in the case of unruly passengers, it also helps clear up a common accusation that Passmore says now comes after many crashes: “The first thing that a lot of people do nowadays is accuse the other person of being on their phone.” What’s more, the newest cabin cameras are wide-angle enough to cover the sides of the car that front and rear lenses miss. “So if somebody keys your car on the side, or if you get T-boned or pulled over by the cops,” Bravy says, “you have an interior cam that can also record on the side.”

Most of the experts we spoke with recommend 2K (1440p) as the minimum resolution you should look for in a dashcam these days and suggest that you don’t even bother with 1080p (standard HD). “2K is kind of the sweet spot right now for both video quality and price,” Bravy says.

The main reason you want better resolution is to capture details at distance. “Most of the [2K] cameras will pick up a license plate easily from 20 feet,” Steinberg says, while “typically a 4K will grab that at 50 or more feet away,” which is the difference between reading the plate of the car that hit you and the one that cut across three lanes and kept going.

For a premium, you can go up to 4K, but make sure you’re getting the real thing: “4K” doesn’t always mean true 4K — sometimes it’s just a bigger image. “What a lot of companies will do is they’ll use a 2K sensor, and then they’ll advertise 4K, and then what they’re doing is they’re just taking the image, and they’re stretching it in software, and they’re interpolating it,” Bravy says. “That doesn’t add any additional detail” because interpolation is just filling in missing pixels with similar-looking pixels rather than displaying more actual video information.

To determine whether or not the camera delivers real 4K, Bravy says, examine the spec sheet and “look for 3840 by 2160 at 30 FPS. If they mention the sensor size or the sensor model, that’s really helpful.” If a brand doesn’t name its sensor or lists an odd resolution or 24 frames per second, “that’s usually a red flag,” says Bravy.

The sensor to look for on dashcam spec sheets (and the one used in most of our recommendations) is the Sony Starvis 2, an image sensor optimized for the low-light and high-contrast scenarios commonly found on the road while driving or parked, day or night. “Sony Starvis sensors are considered the best low-light sensors in the world,” says Steinberg. It means you might actually have a chance at identifying the hit-and-run driver who side-swiped your car or the hooligan who keyed your car while it was parked on your block all night. “Let’s say they have a tattoo on their neck,” says Stefano Loria, owner of Autocraft NYC, a car electronics installer. “You could see what kind of tattoo it is.”

HDR is also important, especially at night, for capturing scenarios — cars moving in the dark, headlights, lit-up license plates — that require different kinds of exposures to be clear, accurate, and usable. With HDR, the camera shoots two pictures with different exposures simultaneously and then merges them. Without HDR, something like a license plate could end up as nothing more than a white blur.

Also look for a circular polarizing filter, or CPL, which cuts the reflection of your own dashboard off the curved windshield glass. This can be “a real big problem with dashcams,” Steinberg says. Some cameras include one; others sell it separately.

Capturing the footage of an accident isn’t sufficient — you also need the footage to be clear and detailed enough to actually see what happened. The field of view, or FOV, tells you how wide an area your camera can record. The wider the angle, the wider the view. Most dashcams have FOV angles between 130 and 160 degrees with an average of about 140 degrees, which should give you a view of multiple highway lanes or a large intersection in case of an accident. Steinberg’s rule: “I wouldn’t accept from the front camera less than 120 degrees.” 140 is better, he continues, but beyond that you get “a lot of fish-eye, a lot of bend at the sides.”

Every camera records while you drive. Parking mode determines whether it keeps watch after you turn the car off. It’s the reason most people walk into Loria’s shop. If someone backs into you and leaves, he says, it’ll have their plate number, and it’ll have the footage of them backing up into you, and then driving away.”

But not all parking modes are created equal. “A lot of dashcams, they’ll cheap out on parking recording,” says Bravy. The most basic version puts the camera to sleep and wakes it when the G-sensor feels a hit, a few seconds too late to capture an incident. “You wind up missing the whole thing,” he says. Look for “buffered” parking mode that records a few seconds in a loop 24/7, which can then be referenced to support any footage activated by a specific trigger event, including motion or impact. Thinkware’s top models have radar, which Choi says “can detect activity before the camera fully wakes up” at a lower power draw than recording all night. BlackVue’s low-power standby draws a single milliamp, which Loria calls “very, very, very low draw.”

There are four ways to power a dashcam: plugged into the cigarette-lighter port on the dash, an onboard battery pack, or via the car’s own battery either over an OBD-II cable connector or hardwired to the car’s fuse box.

“The No. 1 mistake I see is expecting parking mode from a cigarette-lighter install,” Choi says. This type of install is convenient, but the power shuts off with the ignition, meaning this method is a no-go for parking mode. Look instead for an OBD-II cable (which doesn’t work with every car or camera, so check), a hardwire kit (a cable connection right into the fuse box that typically shuts off automatically before it drains your battery), or a separate lithium battery bank that charges while you drive and runs separately from your car battery while you’re parked. “For frequent overnight street parking, I usually prefer the battery-pack route,” Choi says.

Most hardwired cameras have no internal battery, just a capacitor that stores enough charge to upload or save the last file if power cuts. But for those that do have their own battery packs, you’ll want to check them periodically if you live in a hot climate: While lithium batteries hold a charge for a long time, their life spans shorten — and they can sometimes swell or stop working — when exposed to high temperatures.

As for who does the wiring, it depends on how much of an electrician you are. “I recommend professional installation for anyone uncomfortable removing trim panels or working around the fuse box,” says Choi. Loria’s shop charges “$250 and up for installation,” and cautions about trying DIY especially if you have a leather interior. Ronen Yossef, owner of Car Systems Installation in Toronto and a veteran installer since 1999, has seen all kinds of dashcam DIY disasters: overloaded fuses that suddenly make other circuits in the car stop working, rear-camera cables that let water into the trunk, dealers threatening to void warranties. “We see a lot of people who get burned from the situation,” he says. “You want to find the people who do electronics accessories for a living,” not a tint shop that added cameras last year. Choi agrees: “It’s not where I would encourage people to learn by trial and error.”

And whoever installs it, make sure they aim it in the right direction. “So many cameras I see, they’re sort of pointed up at the sky,” Bravy says.

Most dashcams record on and come with a microSD card; if you want more storage, swap in a larger-capacity card. Dashcams record video continuously, however, and they sit exposed in the hot sun, and budget cards aren’t built for 24/7 action.

Buyers typically “find the cheapest memory card on Amazon and try to put it in there, and that’s a recipe for disaster,” says Robert Baller, a dashcam reviewer and tester who publishes his findings on the enthusiast forum DashCamTalk. So buy a high-endurance card made for continuous recording. Given where memory prices are this year, a good card can cost “sometimes more than the dash camera,” jokes Baller, who recommends a card from SanDisk’s Max Endurance line.

While dashcams overwrite old footage to save space on the card, you can typically save important footage manually or in your camera’s app. Many newer dashcams are capable of sensing when a crash has occurred and will automatically prevent that data from being overwritten. To keep your footage extra secure, some dashcams give you the option to record to the cloud, so recordings are backed up virtually, either via your phone while you’re in the car, or using an LTE module. You can also get an external hard drive if you want to keep an archive of all your footage and do a routine file transfer before clearing your microSD card.

Some cameras offer connectivity options that can upload all your video to the cloud, either tethered to your mobile phone or a dedicated LTE modem (the latter is required if you want real-time alerts when you’re away from your car while it’s in parking mode). GPS, which adds speed and location to the video’s metadata, is nice to have, but isn’t available on all cameras. Loria says he has used it to show a customer that they were doing 58mph in a 65mph speed-limit zone when a ticket said otherwise.

Interestingly, not all cameras have screens, making it harder to point them properly, but also, arguably, making them less distracting. And not all dashcams have physical record buttons, worth keeping in mind if you think you’ll sometimes want to manually capture video while you’re driving. Bravy dislikes this approach since he “can’t press the button because I’m doing all this by feel.”

Cameras: Two-channel (front and rear; optional 1080p infrared cabin camera) | Resolution: 2K (2560×1440) at 30fps, front and rear | Sensor: Sony Starvis 2 IMX675, both cameras, with HDR on both | FOV: 140 degrees front, 160 degrees rear (diagonal) | Parking mode: Buffered, with auto event detection, time-lapse, and low-bitrate modes; HK4 hardwire kit ($26) sold separately | Power: Supercapacitor, no battery (optional battery pack, $299) | Storage: microSD up to 512GB, card not included | Extras: 5GHz Wi-Fi, GPS, voice control, 2.4-inch screen, CPL filter optional; 18-month warranty

Bravy says that dash cams with 2K resolution offer the best bang for the buck, and he recommends the Viofo A229, which gives you 2K HDR front and rear courtesy of Starvis 2 chips in both cameras — and costs half of what leading 4K front/2K rear setups do (and is almost as affordable as options that only provide a 1080p rear camera). You get “good video quality, front and rear, also an optional interior cam, which I find really helpful,” Bravy continues. DashCamTalk’s Baller, who has reviewed dashcams since 2019, says the A229 is “one of the best [for] video quality with the best HDR support.”

Top-shelf sensor aside, Bravy points out that the A229 also does parking mode the right way. “Where cheaper cameras sleep and wake a few seconds after an impact, “[the Viofos] monitor continuously,” Bravy says, and “save the clip before the impact, during, and after,” provided you add the HK4 hardwire kit and a memory card. You can also add a battery pack for maximum security.

The 2.4-inch screen makes aiming and menu changes easy even without an app. If you later want to add full interior coverage, Viofo sells infrared 1080p cameras that plug into this unit as an add-on, including the RN210, with a fish-eye lens that provides an ultrawide 210-degree field of view that covers the entire cabin. Yossef, whose shop settled on Viofo after years of trying other brands, sums up the appeal pithily: “They’re not super expensive and they work very well. They’re reliable, quality, long-lasting.”

The one thing the Viofo A229 Plus can’t do is alert you when something happens to your parked car, since it has no LTE module. For that, see the BlackVue below.

Cameras: Two-channel (front and rear) | Resolution: 4K (3840×2160) at 30fps front (also 1440p/60 and 1080p/120), 1080p rear | Sensor: Sony Starvis, 1/1.8-inch, 8MP, f/1.55 front; 2MP f/2.0 rear | FOV: 170 degrees front, 140 rear | Parking mode: Time-lapse and impact-triggered; hardwire kit sold separately | Power: Supercapacitor; rated from –4 to 158°F | Storage: 128GB card included, up to 512GB | Extras: 3.18-inch IPS touchscreen, Wi-Fi 6, GPS mount, voice control, app; 18-month warranty

According to Steinberg, dash cams by the Chinese manufacturer Redtiger have become very popular recently. “We’ve been selling the daylight out of these things,” he says. And that’s for good reason. For less than most of the competition, you get a bona fide 4K front camera, a Sony Starvis sensor, a 1080p rear camera, Wi-Fi 6, and a touchscreen “nearly half an inch [larger than] the competition.” Where other brands bundle in a 64GB card, “Redtiger gets you 128, kind of generous at this price, and it has a big touchscreen.” And the warranty is 18 months — six months longer than Garmin and Thinkware.

The use case Steinberg keeps coming back to is the household with more than one car. “How many families are multi-car families now?” he asks. Put one in the teenager’s car and one in each parent’s, “and since they’ll all be using the same app, it’s very easy to manage what’s going on.” There are some trade-offs, though: The 170-degree front lens sits above Steinberg’s own 140-degree fish-eye threshold, so expect the images to look a little rounded or bubble-like; parking mode needs a hardwire kit (sold separately); and the brand doesn’t have much of a track record yet. “How it’s going to hold up over time, I don’t know,” he says. “But at the price, I have to include it in my list of recommendations, and the [customer] support seems to be there so far.”

Cameras: Three-channel (front, rear, infrared fish-eye cabin camera) | Resolution: 4K (3840×2160) at 30fps front (60fps only with the cabin camera off), 2K at 30fps rear, 2K cabin | Sensor: Sony STARVIS 2 IMX678 8MP front, IMX675 5MP rear and cabin; HDR on all three | FOV: Cabin 210 degrees; front 140; rear 160 degrees| Parking mode: Buffered; Hybrid mode switches from time-lapse or low-bitrate recording to low-power impact detection at a set voltage; requires the HK6 hardwire kit ($33), sold separately; wakes within 2 seconds | Power: Supercapacitor; HK6 kit adds a Bluetooth voltage readout | Storage: microSD; supports an external SSD up to 4TB (about three weeks of footage) | Extras: Wi-Fi 6, USB 3.0, GPS, voice control, screen, front CPL included, multiplexed export; 18-month warranty; no LTE or remote alerts

“If someone wants one of the best all-around setups available right now, I would point them to the Viofo A329S 3CH,” Choi says, and while his store sells it, he’s not alone in his ringing endorsement. Baller and Bravy also put this camera at the top of their lists.

Viofo has put Sony Star is 2 sensors on all three channels with multi-exposure HDR, and Wi-Fi 6 for transferring clips, setting this model apart from the other 4K models in our roundup. Baller singles out the A329’s parking mode, which is built on a newer chipset that lets a car battery, rather than a $300 accessory battery pack, run it overnight. There are a couple of caveats: The hybrid parking mode requires the optional Viofo HK6 kit, and there’s no LTE option, so you can’t get remote alerts. (That said, you also won’t have to worry about not having access to your footage if the camera is stolen since it can automatically store footage on an external SSD drive you can place elsewhere in the car, the only model in this roundup to do so). The A329S has a built-in screen, “which sounds minor until you need to check footage or change a setting at the side of the road without digging through an app,” Choi says.

That third camera, by the way, does more than just watch the driver. The cabin lens is a 210-degree fish-eye, which is wide enough to see out the side windows. “It’s not recording just the inside, but it’s ultrawide, so it also captures off to the side of the vehicle,” Bravy says. “So somebody keys your car on the side, if you get T-boned to the side, if you get pulled over by the cops, you have an interior cam that can also record the side.” That’s one blind spot that a typical two-camera setup doesn’t cover, but in a city where damage often strikes the side of a parked car, it’s a good reason to spend $500. Bravy runs one in his own car and says it’s “some of the best video quality I’ve ever seen.”

And here’s a nifty variant: If you don’t need interior coverage, you can still benefit from the third channel with the Viofo A329T, which swaps out the cabin camera for a dedicated telephoto lens aimed at license plates (Bravy has installed that setup in one of his own cars).

Cameras: Two-channel (front and rear) | Resolution: 4K (3840×2160) at 30fps front with HDR, 4K at 30fps rear | Sensor: Sony STARVIS 2 IMX678 front and rear | FOV: 146 degrees diagonal, both cameras | Parking mode: Power Saving standby (under 1mA), motion and time-lapse; 10-second pre-buffer on events; low-voltage cutoff adjustable 11.8–12.5V; high-temperature cutoff around 167°F | Power: Hardwire cable and 12-volt USB-C adapter included; OBD-II cable $22; Ultra Battery accessory for extended parking coverage | Storage: 64GB card included, up to 1TB; 5GB free cloud storage | Extras: Dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, touch-sensor record button, speaker; optional LTE module (CM100GLTE); screenless; 2-year warranty

Unlike all of the other 4K dashcams we considered, the Elite 10 offers 4K HDR cameras front and rear. Most rivals have only a 4K front camera with a 2K unit in the rear. And courtesy of Starvis 2 sensors in both cameras, “the video quality is great,” says Bravy, “on par with the Viofos and the Vueroids.” Baller thinks Viofo and Vueroid have the edge on HDR processing, so a license plate under direct headlights may be a little harder to discern than on some of its competitors.

While most dashcams don’t have any way of sending you a notification since they don’t offer LTE even as an option, BlackVue has long offered cloud connectivity on their dashcams. Bravy says that if you really want to keep an eye on what’s going on in your parked vehicle, BlackVue is the way to go: The live view, he says “is almost real-time.” BlackVue has had a cloud feature “forever, effectively, in the dashcam market,” Baller says. “They’re kind of the king when it comes to that.”

A BlackVue dash cam with the LTE module, or connected to a Wi-Fi hotspot in the car, tells you what’s happening while it’s happening. Even if a thief succeeds in stealing the camera itself, a clip, including the seconds before the event, is uploaded to the car before the camera can be removed. Impact alerts and event uploads are free; what you pay for (from $3.99 a month, $7.99 for unlimited) is live-view and playback from your phone.

And it’s easy to operate. Loria’s favorite detail is the camera setup: “It’s like a wave and a tap, and it connects,” and then he mounts the unit “right behind” the mirror “where you don’t see it.”

Cameras: Two-channel (front and rear, with optional infrared cabin camera or LTE module via the USB-C port) | Resolution: 4K (3840×2160) at 30fps front (or 1440p at 60), 2K (2560×1440) at 30fps rear; H.265 | Sensor: 8.4MP 1/1.8-inch front, 5.14MP 1/2.8-inch rear (Sony Starvis 2 IMX678/IMX675, per Thinkware), dual HDR, “Super Night Vision 4.0” | FOV: 147 degrees front, 156 degrees rear (diagonal) | Parking mode: Built-in radar with motion detection, time-lapse, and energy-saving modes; battery and thermal protection | Power: Hardwire or OBD-II; OBD-II cable included; supercapacitor; rated 14 to 140°F | Storage: 64GB card included, up to 512GB | Extras: Dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, ADAS alerts, voice guide, CPL filter and heat-blocking film included; optional LTE module; screenless; 12-month warranty

For regular George Costanzas who make the most of alternate-side parking and want to get daytime dent-and-runs and nocturnal break-ins on the record, three of our experts recommend this camera. It’s the only camera in this group with radar, which can monitor continuously while using less energy than a camera in standby in low-power mode when a car is parked. So, instead of waiting for a jolt to wake it, the U3000 Pro monitors the space around the parked car and starts recording when something approaches. Not only does radar draw less power when something’s detected moving by your vehicle, but it awakens the camera before an impact occurs and starts recording. “Radar,” Choi adds, “can help capture more of what happened around the vehicle while using less power than leaving the camera recording at full tilt all night.”

It’s exceedingly sensitive. “It immediately knows if the car has been touched or anything like that,” says Steinberg, who particularly loves what the U3000 Pro does after dark. The Sony Starvis 2 front sensor “pulls every bit of light it can from a nighttime scene. So reflected light, light that’s farther away … it pulls it in, and it’s quite remarkable,” he says, which is ideal for “somebody [who’s] really concerned about low light because they do a lot of night driving.” Thinkware also offers an LTE module so even if you’re not in the car when something happens, the radar can send an alert to your phone and save a clip to the cloud. The downside? Bravy thinks that Thinkware’s image processing doesn’t live up to its hardware: “Their HDR, their video quality, is not as good as what I see from some of the competition.” If you care most about street parking scenarios, though, video quality is less important when the car isn’t moving.

Cameras: Two- or Three-channel (front and rear; optional 1080p infrared cabin camera) | Resolution: 4K (3840×2160) front, 2K (2560×1440) rear | Sensor: Sony Starvis 2 IMX678 front, IMX675 rear, with HDR and an “Infinite Plate Capture” mode | FOV: 151 degrees front, 160 degrees rear | Parking mode: Impact and motion, time-lapse, Extreme Low Power standby (1mA, wakes in under a second); DURASHIFT heat mode drops to low-power recording instead of shutting down | Power: Hardwire cable, fuse taps, and CPL filter included; low-voltage cutoff | Storage: microSD, high-endurance A2/U3/V30 card required| Extras: 2.3-inch LCD, Wi-Fi, GPS, Vueroid Hub app with AI plate restoration and face/plate blurring; made in South Korea; no LTE or remote alerts

Every dashcam lives on a windshield, and any car parked outside in the summertime (especially in a sunny, hot climate) becomes an oven. Most cameras handle that by shutting off, but Vueroid instead goes into Extreme Low-Power mode, avoiding overheating and helping save your car’s battery life in the process. It’s perfect for Phoenix, Houston — or a Brooklyn lot with no shade.

In a heat wave, says Bravy, the S1 “will switch and go to a low-power parking recording mode, where it’s no longer monitoring continuously — it’s in a sleep state. If it detects an impact, it wakes up in a second, begins recording, and then goes back to sleep. And then once it cools off, it goes back to normal recording.” Baller has found the same in his testing. With the S1, he says, “you don’t have to really worry about your vehicle battery.”

But aside from superlative battery life and heat resistance, Baller says the S1 specifically has “very good video quality for the front camera, and a lot of parking mode options.” You get Sony Starvis 2 sensors, 4K front and 2K rear, a hardwire kit, fuse taps, and a polarizing filter in the box. The brand is new to American shelves but not to the dashcam space: It comes from a Korean company that has spent two decades building cameras for other brands and is well-respected within the industry: “Viofo and Vueroid, those are the ones I tend to recommend,” says Baller. The S1 has no LTE support, but the app has an AI plate-restoration feature that can sharpen a blurry photo of a license plate post-incident.

entry.title: The 10 Very Best Outdoor Heaters
entry.summary: Whether you’re stoop-sitting, RV-ing, or hosting an outdoor event.
entry.content:
As a former van-lifer who has camped in the cold for months at a time, I’m a firm believer in using heaters outdoors. They are ideal for keeping RVs and tents warm or, as many people discovered during the pandemic, for hosting gatherings and dinner parties in whatever outside space you have. You can take an outdoor heater fishing at the lake or just sit out on the stoop with your friends on chillier nights.

To find the best outdoor heaters, I tested a few myself while also consulting hospitality professionals, contractors, and folks who just love keeping warm to find out more about their favorites. Below you’ll find a range of options, from propane-powered gizmos for RV living to a bronze column of flames that’ll make your patio feel like a fancy hotel courtyard — and even an alternative for those who’d rather not use a heater at all.

Updated on November 25, 2026
I’ve updated these picks with the latest pricing and availability.

There are a couple things to consider when choosing an outdoor heater, says David Heiman, the senior director of training at Phoenix’s the Refrigeration School Inc. The first, of course, is location: “Determine the size of the space that will be heated,” he says. If you’re just a few bodies around a blanket or a campsite, a smaller tabletop or camping heater should suffice, but if you’re looking for something to provide warmth in an outdoor dining area that can fit slightly larger groups, you might opt for a larger freestanding heater (which can be moved — but not as easily, given their hulking frames). If you’re looking to heat a larger outdoor space you use a lot, you can get mounted heaters that will require a bit more installation but then become a permanent fixture.

As with air conditioners, outdoor heaters measure power in BTUs, with models that put out more BTUs generally better at warming bigger swathes of space. As Andrews explains, “An outdoor heater that reaches up to 48,000 BTU could keep eight to ten people on a regular-size deck or patio quite warm.” All of the non-portable heaters recommended below feature BTU outputs of between 40,000 and 48,000 — because of this, choosing a larger outdoor heater, as many of our experts note, can largely come down to aesthetics.

​​In addition to considering your space, Andrews says you’ll want to think about the type of fuel source. Propane-fueled and electric are two of the most common and user-friendly styles of heaters. Scott Gorky, the president of Atlas Party Rentals, says that while electric heaters are more reliable (as opposed to propane, which will eventually run out), propane heaters can be more effective because they emit radiant heat (meaning they warm the people and objects in outdoor areas much in the same way the sun heats our planet) rather than forced-air heat (the system used by most indoor heaters, wherein the heater warms the air around it). “You can stand in a circle around a propane heater, but with an electric one, you’ve got to kind of be in front of it because electric heaters only point heat in one direction,” he says.

Intended use: Camping, RVs, small outdoor gatherings | Output: 4,000 to 9,000 BTUs | Fuel source: 1 lb. propane cylinder

For affordability, ease of use, and toasty radiant heating power, I don’t think you can do better than a Mr. Heater. I relied on one during an eight-month van-life trip that included a fair bit of frosty wintertime camping, and the brand is also beloved by experts like Taylor Kalsey, a community manager for camping platform the Dyrt, who agrees that its heaters are a must-have for cold-weather RV camping. If run on high, a one-pound propane canister can power this model for up to three hours; on a lower setting, you’ll get more like five. Outdoors, Kalsey says, this should be enough for “four to five people sitting around it in a close circle.” Strategist editor Maxine Builder is a fan too, and not just for the camping trips she takes. She says the Buddy “puts out serious heat” and is a cinch to use: “All you have to do is screw on the propane canister, click the pilot light on, and, once it catches, set it to either high or low.” She finds it so effective that she “convinced my husband’s mom to buy two more for outdoor hangs.” The heater comes with an automatic safety shut-off function should it accidentally tip over or detect low-oxygen levels, which is great if you’re using it to work in a cold garage or heat up an RV (but be sure to ventilate the space either way).

﻿Intended use: Camping, hunting and fishing, RVs | Output: 3,800 BTUs | Fuel source: 1 lb. propane cylinder

For couples or solo winter outdoorspeople, I love the Buddy’s smaller version, appropriately called the Little Buddy. It’s only a foot tall, and you can adjust the angle of its heating element to direct warmth where you need it. It has a run time of just over five hours with a one-pound propane tank. This was the Mr. Buddy that I used when van living, and it was perfect for frosty nights out in the desert: it’s plenty warm and intuitive to use and was compact enough to store in a small space. Now that I’m back in Brooklyn, I’ve used it for cold-weather stoop hangs. As with the larger model, the Little Buddy has a low-oxygen sensor and accidental tip-over switch.

﻿Intended use: Industrial spaces | Output: 45,000 BTUs | Fuel source: Any propane tank

While this Mr. Heater model is less sleek-looking than those above, it’s no less effective. The Tank Top comes recommended by Cooper Mitchell, the founder of the website Garage Gym Reviews, who says that this outdoor heater is a great affordable way to heat an (almost always) uninsulated space like a garage — which, as his website suggests, are utilized for far more than just storing junk (especially these days). According to Mitchell, who says it often gets “below freezing” where he lives in Missouri, “it disperses heat widely” thanks to its output of 30,000–45,000 BTUs. As its name suggests, this heater attaches to the top of a propane tank — it can fit as small as a 20-pound tank or as large as a 100-pound tank — and will last about nine to ten hours at full blast on a 20-pounder. “For the cost of both the unit and the propane fuel, it will do an incredible job” heating up a one-car garage turned gym or art studio or whatever, Mitchell says. (As it’s technically meant for outdoor use, Mitchell suggests opening your garage a few inches “simply to allow airflow for the exhaust from the propane to have a place to go.”)

Intended use: Camping | Output: 3,333 BTUs | Fuel source: Butane tank

Outdoorswoman Brittany Alexandria Parks uses this cute little camping Kovea to warm up her tent on chilly mornings and nights. She initially considered buying the Mr. Heater Little Buddy above but decided that it was too bulky to pack in the trunk of her Kia Soul. Indeed, while the Cupid is plenty warm, its main draw might just be its compact size and unusually good looks. “Aesthetics are important to me,” Parks admits. “It feels silly, but I do try and keep things at the campsite as minimal as possible, so they don’t distract from the natural environment.” She likes that the heater comes with a hard plastic carry case — “like the old-school Coleman lanterns came in.” Note that this heater, unlike its fellow portables above, lacks an automatic tip-over switch, but it is much harder to knock over in the first place, as it’s positioned closer to the ground on a metal stand that can be angled to direct warmth wherever you want it. Just make sure to use it in a ventilated space and away from flammable objects and fabrics. “I put it in the corner of my tent, being sensible and making sure there’s space around it,” says Parks. “It’s super-stable, and I haven’t had any issue with it tipping over.”

Intended use: Outdoor entertaining | Output: 48000 BTUs | Fuel source: 20lb propane cylinder

Andrews says her favorite heater for backyards and gardens is easily this seven-foot model from Hampton Bay. It uses a 20-pound propane tank and has a 48,000-BTU burner that will suit spaces of up to 200 square feet — and you can adjust the temperature. I like this model for its affordability combined with heating power: Pricier models will have added features like wheels or more stylish metal encasements, but this one has a sturdy stainless-steel frame that, at 33 pounds, is still light enough to move around, even for non–garage gym rats.

Intended use: Outdoor entertaining | Output: 42,000 BTUs | Fuel source: 20lb propane cylinder

And here’s a patio heater you’ll find yourself inventing outdoor winter social events for — just to show it off. Justin Grimes, the managing director of nine boutique hotels in Maine, uses Lava Heat Italia’s pyramid-style Capri A-line heater on his property for outdoor dining. The six-foot-tall unit has “an attractive bronze finish,” he says, that’s rustproof. Plus, it can cover about 36 square feet, which gives plenty of space to party. One propane tank will last for around 12 hours with 360-degree infrared heat, and the “column of flame” design looks pretty damn cool. Or hot.

Intended use: Outdoor entertaining | Output: 40,000 BTUs | Fuel source: 20lb propane cylinder

Though still an investment, at a third of the cost, I think this heater is a worthy dupe for the Lava Heat one above. Plus, its wheels make it incredibly simple to rearrange in any outdoor space. “You can just tip [the heater] and steer it to where you want it,” one Amazon reviewer writes. “It is easy to assemble, easy to ignite and looks classy.” Many other purchasers praise its sleek display of flames: One calls it “mesmerizing to watch.” But despite its fiery majesty, a fourth reviewer assures that the design is child-friendly. “I liked the fact that the grills that go on the four sides do not heat up. I have twin 10-year-olds that are already very curious about the flames, but the side grills are cool to the touch.”

Intended use: Camping and outdoor entertaining | Output: 7 hours of high-flame burn time on one battery charge | Fuel source: Firewood, battery-powered fan

The problem with most backyard firepits is that you have to, well, build a fire to make them work. BioLite makes this an accessible skill even for non-outdoorsy types with its clever built-in USB rechargeable fan, which keeps flames burning at three different intensities while reducing smoke. Strategist contributing writer James Lynch purchased one of these “tech-bro” firepits during peak pandemic lockdown, and was amazed at how easy it was to create roaring flames. “After lighting newspaper or other kindling under the wood, instead of causing yourself to hyperventilate, just tap a button in the app, and airflow in the burn chamber increases automatically,” he explains. “If you want more heat, just turn the fan up. You don’t have to stoke the fire to keep it burning either. Add wood and the FirePit takes care of the rest.” While I haven’t used one of these myself, I’ve cooked a few camp meals on BioLite’s similar wood-fired stove, and can attest that a fan truly makes all the difference.

Intended use: Outdoor entertaining | Output: 26 hours on low, 6 hours on high per 20-pound tank | Fuel source: Propane

If you prefer firepit ambience but don’t want to take the extra step of building a wood fire, why not try a gas firepit? The Fireside360 is Ninja’s first outdoor firepit and is built with the same efficiency and easy-to-use controls as everything else from the brand. It comes ready to go (just pop in an included battery for the starter and hook up the fuel) and you’ll be warm in seconds.

Strategist contributor Maggie Slepian found that the Ninja can keep four people seated around the pit comfortably warm. As with other gas firepits this really a gas heater that uses flames for effect — the fire itself loses a little heat upward, while the heat ring that radiates useful warmth outward towards you and your guests. The Fireside360 can run for up to 26 hours on a 20-pound propane tank and a weather cover is available separately.

Intended use: Outdoor entertaining | Output: 20,472 BTUs | Fuel source: Electric

For the best mounted heater, I turned to the people who, after years of pandemic dining, know the truth about outdoor heating: restaurant owners. Gowanus Gardens partner Kelly Hayes sung the praises of Infratech’s 4,000- and 5,000-watt mounted outdoor heaters, which emit radiant heat and have kept the venue’s outdoor-dining space cozy since winter 2020. “Back then, we were the only game in town,” she says. “All of our friends who owned other bars came here to drink, even when the weather was frozen.” Two other folks recommended Infratech’s mounted heaters: Shaun Gotterbarn, a project architect at Alisberg Parker Architects, and Michael Dean, outdoor-living consultant and founder of Pool Research, who pointed us to this 6,000-watt model, which would be great if you’re outfitting a smaller space and don’t wish to buy more than one heater. Measuring about five feet in length, its maximum output of 6,000 watts means it can keep about four to six people warm, as long as they’re sitting or standing near it. Dean notes that because it’s infrared, the heater is “not only energy-efficient but very quiet when it’s on.” He appreciates the “low-profile look of the heater itself,” which he says is “great for homeowners who don’t want the heater to be too visible or noticeable — a priority for many people.” Of Infratech’s heaters, Gotterbarn adds, “They integrate into spaces very well, and our clients have been very happy with them.” The unit can be controlled by a switch and even comes with an option to integrate it with smart-home devices.

Intended use: Home | Heat range: Up to 140﻿℉ | Power source: AC

When Milk Bar Park Slope co-owner Kylie Sachs sought to improve her café’s courtyard set up in 2020, propane and electric heaters were too expensive — not to mention the ongoing energy bills they’d require. She was already using these cozy heating pads at home, so she purchased more for Milk Bar’s outdoor diners, with whom they were an instant hit. I am a regular customer myself and loved using the pads so much that I asked Sachs about them. “It was an affordable but highly effective solution,” she explains. “Sometimes people sit on one and have another one on their shoulders.” Reminiscent of heated car seats, the pads offer a direct-contact heat during chilly brunches. They’re washable, and Sachs says that when one of her pads stopped working, PureRelief was happy to replace it free of charge.

entry.title: The Best Artificial Christmas Trees, According to People Whose Taste We Trust
entry.summary: “It’s like a giant jewel in your living room.”
entry.content:
Let’s get the obvious out of the way: There’s probably no scent stick or can of room spray that will fully capture the spirit of a real Christmas tree. It’s a smell that immediately evokes images of gingerbread houses and peppermint candy canes. But that doesn’t mean having one is without its problems — from fallen needles and having to water it to figuring out the proper disposal procedures (or even dealing with allergies). That’s where the right artificial Christmas tree comes in.

With an artificial tree, you still get all the holly-jolly joyfulness of a real one without the needle-dropping expiration date. You might even save yourself some bucks for years to come (as long as you have somewhere to store it in the offseason). If it’s your first time going faux and you’re wondering where to start, you’ve come to the right place. I asked set decorators, professional organizers, interior designers, and all-around Christmas enthusiasts about theirs. You’ll find everything from a tree that starred in a Hallmark movie to another that’s a “profane pink number.” And if you’re looking for Christmas-tree decorations, we have guides to the best tree toppers and tree skirts, too.

Updated on October 28, 2026
﻿There are new recommendations in here, including the Balsam Hill Silverado Slim and Terrain Artificial Pre-Lit Alpine Fir. I added testing notes for the Balsam Hill Balsam Fir and updated prices and checked stock for all the other artificial trees on this list.

Available in 5.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 8-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here): unlit, LED color + clear lights, clear incandescent lights, LED clear lights, twinkly light show, and LED clear fairy lights

In the artificial-tree world, Balsam Hill rules. Interior designers, set decorators, and Christmas enthusiasts all sing the brand’s praises, largely because Balsam Hill’s trees don’t look fake-fake. “Some trees just look like plastic,” says Erin Swift, founder of the holiday-decorating firm Holiday Workroom. If you want a hyperrealistic artificial tree, she says, “the answer is simple: Balsam Hill. Always Balsam Hill.”

Balsam Hill trees aren’t cheap: They start at $399 for a Norwegian Grand Fir and average between $549 to $599 for a Classic Evergreen or Vancouver Spruce. A Scotch Pine will cost you even more, at $1,199. “Buy on Black Friday” — when there’s a sitewide discount of up to 50 percent off — was an oft-repeated piece of advice I heard from my sources. The brand’s Amazon storefront often has markdowns, too. But the final price will depend on the tree’s height — many are available from 4.5 feet up to 12 feet — and the lights you pick (Balsam Hill’s bulb guide is helpful for this). Every Balsam Hill artificial tree comes with a storage bag — so you don’t have to shove your investment back into a cardboard box after Christmas — and protective gloves to wear while fluffing the branches. It’s also worth noting that Balsam Hill has branch samples to compare — buying the kit is credited toward your purchase of a full-size tree — and you’re getting a three-year warranty.

The Balsam Fir, which is inspired by balsam firs in Maine, is a best seller, and it’s the most-recommended artificial tree here. I understand why after trying it myself recently: Assembly requires a few minutes and the most work you’re doing is tweaking branches just where you need them to be. When I pressed down on the foot pedal that turns on the tree’s LED clear bulbs for the first time, I couldn’t help feeling merry and bright. Interior designer Betsy Burnham likes the ambience and decorates hers with ornaments including “the tin boats my son used to love as a little kid, the carved family of porcupines my daughter always hung together, and the mini Eiffel Tower that’s always too heavy to sit right, but we use it anyway.”

Available in 3-, 4-, 6.5, 7.5-, and 9-foot heights

Target’s in-house holiday line, Wondershop, is full of inexpensive trees. Because it’s a seasonal shop (like its Halloween Hyde & Eek), stock moves fast — and might not come back for the next holiday season. Thankfully, this Alberta Spruce has, and now comes in different heights: 3, 4, 6.5, 7, and 9 feet. In the old apartment of e-commerce consultant (and my former boss) Brittany Nims, this tree stood between her now-husband’s desk and the entertainment console in their living room, which was very small (even by Brooklyn standards). Nims packed on the sparkle while decorating it, adding mini disco balls, a glittery star topper, and sequined, faux-fur-trimmed skirt. “There’s something about a glowing Christmas tree that’s just so cheerful,” she says.

Available in 5-, 7- and 9-foot heights

“I used to be morally opposed to artificial trees, but my husband is allergic to pine, which left me no other choice when we moved in together,” says Carrie Wittmer, author of First Famous Christmas. Moving into a then-new apartment with high ceilings in 2023, Wittmer decided — after “several years of owning a pitiful but hardworking Target tree” — to get a nine-foot Terrain Alpine Fir (which comes in five- and seven-feet versions too). At Christmastime, it resides in a corner between her dining table and kitchen. “I think the best Christmas trees are ones that feel like they fit into the space naturally,” she says. “Once decorated, it feels quite full. Its slim silhouette makes my weird collection of ornaments stand out more than they would in a thicker, denser tree.” (Her holiday-scented candles “make up for the lack of Christmas tree smell.”)

Available in 4-, 6-, 7-, 8-, 10-, and 12-foot heights

Prop stylist Alexandra Massillon used National Tree Company’s Dunhill Fir for a food-service holiday campaign. It’s “reasonably priced and honestly looks really good,” she says. “I don’t want to say that next to Balsam Hill that it looks exactly the same, but if you have a gift for decorating a tree, no one will notice the difference.”

Stefania Orrù, director of production at Eater, used to own fakes that were best described as “Charlie Brown–y.” It was a YouTube video that persuaded her to get a Dunhill Fir. “It was a steal,” considering how costly an artificial tree can be, says Orrù. It arrives unlit, which means you can change out the lights as you wish. And the needles are “pretty pliable in terms of positioning,” according to Orrù.

Also available in 4-, 4.5-, 6-, 6.5-, 7-, 7.5-, 9-, 10-, 12-, and 14-foot heights with the following pre-lit options: unlit, clear, multicolor, and dual-color

As long as Carrie Courogen, author of Miss May Does Not Exist, has lived in New York, she’s “gone through all the pathetic-tree phases: no tree at all, lights on a random plant, tiny table-top fir.” When she started researching artificial trees, the Kingswood Fir came up on this very site (our writer Brenley Goertzen kept it between a couch and a fireplace in her old apartment). It’s ideal for Courogen’s studio apartment, where “I don’t have a ton of space for something big, both when it’s up and when it’s time to store it.” It has shed minimally between Christmases, but she’s “consistently surprised by how well it fluffs out in spite of its compact nature.” And it’s “comically easy” to set up, taking her no more than ten minutes of “maneuvering to get it looking in good shape.” For someone who grew up in a “very passionate real-Christmas-tree house,” it works. “It obviously gives fake tree during the day, but at night when the lights are low and it’s glowing in the corner, I’ll admit, it comes pretty close to the real thing,” she says. 

Available in 6.5-, 7-, 7.5-, 9-, and 12-foot heights and either clear or dual-color lights

Our writer Kitty Guo grew up with an artificial tree that her dad put up every year — and this year, she put up one of her own. Guo set up the Downswept Douglas Fir (sent to her by National Tree Company to test) a few weeks ago and says that it was “extremely easy” to assemble. The tree’s parts slot together in a puzzlelike way, and the branches fall into place naturally. “All you need to do is a bit of fluffing and you’re done,” she says.

The Downswept Douglas Fir comes in heights of 6.5, 7, 7.5, 9, and 12 feet. Guo keeps her 6.5-foot tree at the foot of a staircase and says that the “pencil slim” silhouette prevents it from feeling in the way, even with the tree’s tall height. You can choose between clear or multicolored LED bulbs for the tree’s lights. “There are ten different options that you can toggle between with the foot pedal, and the lights will change colors, twinkle gently, or flash quickly in a kaleidoscopic whirl,” Guo says. She’s been buying baubles to fill out the tree ever since it was delivered: “I can definitely see this tree being the centerpiece of my Christmas decorations for years to come.”

Available in 6.5-, 7.5-, and 9-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit and LED clear lights

Massillon has rented Balsam Hill’s trees for shoots — and remembers the box for a Douglas Fir “was beat up because it has been used over and over for 15-plus years by me and every other prop stylist or set designer in NYC.” Maybe that’s because setting it up is easy, says Massillon: “I hate the other artificial trees because there can be so many branches that get bent and flat; it is a nightmare.” In comparison, when the parts of the Douglas Fir are stacked, “the leaves kind of fall into place … like an umbrella.”

Available in 4.5-, 5.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 8-, 9-, 10-, 11-, 12-, 15-, and 18-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit, LED color and LED color + clear lights, and LED clear lights

The Vermont White Spruce is another Balsam Hill bestseller. It’s meant to resemble the true white spruces of New England. Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio, who was sent a sampler kit, says the branches on the Vermont White Spruce are ever-so-slightly darker with pointier needle tips than those on the Balsam Fir’s. Joanna Douglas, the former director of branded content at Vox Media, says guests always compliment hers for how real it looks. That was especially important to her, as someone who was formerly against going faux. Douglas praises the branches’ bendability, allowing her to arrange and rearrange them as needed. Hers is decorated with photos of her cats depicted as angels — they were once naughty, nibbling on the needles and sipping on trunk water of her real trees, but are now “completely disinterested” in messing with her fake.

Available in 4.5-, 5.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 8-, 9-, 10-, 12-, 15-, and 18-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit, LED color + clear lights, clear incandescent lights, LED clear lights, twinkly light show, and C7 multicolor LED

Balsam Hill’s Classic Blue Spruce was featured on the set of Hallmark’s One Royal Holiday. Fittingly, the movie’s set decorator, Christi Whiteley, calls it “majestic.” Another fan is Lauren Ragan, director of ad operations at Vox Media. The real-looking needles on this tree take a while to arrange the first few times — each branch has needles arranged in a sort of fan shape, and they need to be pushed out and down — “but after some time, it gets easier and easier, my husband tells me,” Ragan says. After pulling the trigger on the “onetime investment” four Christmases ago, she hasn’t looked back. Ragan goes for a “nice dressing” of different-colored ornaments on the tree, a compromise with her husband. Her in-laws, who are big on Christmas, have theirs “doused in ornaments,” a tradition her husband embraced before.

Available in 6-, 7-, 8-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit, LED color + clear lights, twinkly light show, ultrabright clear LED, and starlight twinkle LED

This is the first artificial tree designer Jess Knauf has owned as an adult, and it’s a far cry from “the very plasticky one my parents had in the ’90s.” She says it’s a cinch to put together, and the branches have plenty of space for ornament hanging. “We will be on year six this year,” she says. During each of those years, she’s filled with her collection of “vintage, unfashionable but sentimental ornaments,” and that this year, her topper might be a new floppy bow.

Available in 5-, 6-, 7-, 8-, and 9-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit and LED clear lights

If you want a realistic tree that nonetheless looks a bit frosty — and isn’t flocked — Trolio recommends Balsam Hill’s Sanibel Spruce. “It’s one of my absolute favorites of the handful of Balsam Hill trees I’ve acutally seen in person,” she says. Plus it “very much matches the product photo on the site,” which isn’t always the case when it comes to artificial trees. The tips of the needles on this tree are a bit lighter in color, and the branch tips are especially lifelike. “One of the more obvious giveaways that makes a tree look fake is how the needles look,” explains professional organizer Britnee Tanner. The Sanibel Spruce resembles the evergreen in her yard instead of the “loose, sparse, and floppy” look of other fakes. Trolio agrees: “There are a good number of tips per branch” with longer ends that allow for “excellent ornament distribution.” (An important note: It comes pre-fluffed with memory-wired arms that fan into place, according to the company, though Trolio notes that you should still plan to do a good bit of finishing on your own.) Even after a few Christmases, Tanner still considers it to be her best buy for the holidays.

Available in 6.5-, 7.5-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): LED color + clear lights, LED clear lights, and twinkly light show

This is the narrow version of Balsam Hill’s famed Fraser Fir (46 inches wide versus 60 inches wide for a 7.5-foot-tall tree). Selina van den Brink, a freelance set decorator, used this tree for the Oscar-winning film Green Book. She needed something that would last for the entire weekslong shoot and “wouldn’t drop needles while being decorated,” settling on Balsam Hill’s Fraser fir after doing a quick poll of fellow set decorators. “It just has all the characteristics of a real tree,” she says. “It’s not too perfect — with an organic quality to the manufactured branches.” It was featured in a traditional tree-decorating scene, with star Viggo Mortensen coming home for Christmas “just in time to celebrate with his family,” so “the tree was a very big deal,” van den Brink explains.

Available in 5.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights; full , slim, or wide shapes, and the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit, clear incandescent lights, LED clear lights, LED multi-lights, LED color + clear lights, and twinkly light show

Available in 7.5-, 9-, and 10-foot heights, and either of the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here): LED color + clear lights or LED clear lights

Most artificial trees break down so you can store them in a box. The Flip Trees from Balsam Hill are designed to “flip” open on a rolling stand for even easier assembly. (See a video of how it works here.) It’s a feature that prop stylist Andrea Greco considers a “game changer.” (It also helps her rationalize the trees’ price tags.) Greco has owned the Red Spruce for over a decade and also uses them on sets — for one photo op, she covered the tree in hundreds of handmade gardenias dusted with glitter and garlands of paper leaves. She likes the idea of decorating it with a New York City theme, complete with Chrysler Building and Statue of Liberty, vintage subway tokens, and a giant rat.

Available in 6.5- or 7.5-foot heights and a pink version

Another big name to know in faux is King of Christmas. Its traditional and nontraditional trees are similar to Balsam Hill’s (with cheaper starting prices). Trolio had the chance to try out the King of Christmas’s Duchess (in a now sold-out flocked Barbie pink, but the blue version is still available). The color makes an obvious statement, and the settings on the dimmable light bulbs are another show in themselves — including one that Trolio describes as “very ‘dance party’ flashy.” Because of the flocking on the branches, the tree looks much fuller. “Think of thickening mascara on eyelashes,” Trolio says. Beware that upon opening, the tree has a slightly musty smell and sheds during assembly. “It wasn’t terrible, but there was a decent dusting,” she warns. Luckily, it was easy to clean up any fallen flocking with a vacuum. Like Balsam Hill, King of Christmas includes a storage bag and two-year warranty on every tree.

King of Christmas also makes a tabletop tree with lights that remind me of little stars (I kept one on my fireplace mantel all of last December). But inventory is low, so don’t dillydally.

Available in 4.5-, 6-, 7.5-, or 9-foot heights

Once a traditionalist, Strategist contributor Ivy Pochoda “left the fake spruce and tinsel trees behind” for what she describes as a “profane pink number” back in 2021. Even though the tree seemed frivolous at first, it’s well made — sturdy and plush and “filled the living room with shiny pink delight,” she says. Fluffed to its fullest, it “swallows lights and ornaments” — Pochoda decorates the tree with string lights, silver garland, and vintage ornaments from Christopher Radko and Kurt Adler alongside boxed wine and disco-mirror-ball ornaments. She’s since become known as the “person with the pink tree” in her neighborhood. “People paused as they passed my window. They went out of their way to take a look,” Pochoda says.

Available in 5- and 7-foot heights with the following colors and pre-lit options: silver with white lights, gold with white lights, and silver with color lights

“I know it’s fake, but it embraces the fakeness,” says Greco of this Martha Stewart tinsel tree. It reminds her of the retro ones from the ’50s and ’60s: “You know, silver could look tacky, but this does not.” She covered “the whole thing in disco balls” once and is thinking of adorning it with peacock and peach ornaments this year, but appreciates that it could go undecorated. “It’s like a giant jewel in your living room,” she says. “There are no sparse areas — you have to fluff it out, but it’s pure silver.”

If MacKinley Jade Lutes-Adlhoch, writer of the newsletter Yeehawt, could, she’d leave a Christmas tree up year-round: “There’s no way I’d sacrifice having one,” adds Lutes-Adlhoch. “But I have zero room for a wide base anywhere in my apartment.” Not that it’s a problem with this Homcom tree, which goes in a “corner around existing furniture without having to rearrange the whole living room.” You “can’t use a tree skirt because there’s no extra room at the base” (her tree is between an armchair and dresser too). But it’s a price she’s willing to pay for convenience’s sake — and she estimates it takes about 30 minutes to set up. Another bonus: Her cat Tofu, who’d “be thrilled to vomit up pine needles,” isn’t able to climb it. “While the most tenacious of cats could certainly still figure out a way to break every precious ornament, my own cat gave up pretty quickly with this tree,” she says.

Available in 6- and 7-foot heights, and with either of the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): LED clear lights or LED multi-lights

Balsam Hill’s Fifth Avenue Flatback was the tree I used last Christmas. It’s convincing enough that I didn’t even miss the fresh-pine smell of a real tree. But the biggest selling point of the Flatback is that, well, the back is flat. You’re still getting all of the fullness of a real tree in the front, but this tree can stand flush against a wall. It’s ideal for small spaces like mine, where I can only fit a tree between my staircase and the couch.

I also loved that the Flatback assembled (and disassembled) quickly. Because I didn’t have to think about a full 360-degree view, I could cut down on some decorating time, too. Just note: You’ll want to measure the bottom carefully for a tree skirt — I used a standard-size 48-inch one on mine, and had to tuck it around the trunk rather awkwardly. But I’m planning on getting something better-fitting this for coming Christmas.

Available in 4.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights with LED clear fairy lights (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference)

This was the the first Balsam Hill tree Trolio bought for herself (after previously inheriting a hand-me-down in a different style). Though in the end “a fake is still a fake,” Trolio says she chose the “sparse-on-purpose, pre-lit” design specifically for displaying certain ornaments. “I have become a way too over-the-top-Christmas-ornament person. I own hundreds and can’t stop buying them,” she admits.

This Alpine Balsam Fir has a place in the corner of her dining room as a “theme tree” holding her collections of pickle and pretzel ornaments. Since the branches aren’t especially full, the wires for the lights are a bit more visible, so Trolio advises that you be extra thoughtful about what kinds of ornaments you’re hanging — and mindful about getting the right “drop.” (On the same note, she recommends using a tree skirt instead of a tree collar, as the branches don’t go very low on the trunk and a skirt does a better job of hiding the flat metal base.) As for assembly, the tree “goes together super-easily, and the light connectors are built into the sections of the trunk so you don’t have to plug them together separately,” she explains.

This miniature tinseled tree isn’t intended to be a dupe of a real Christmas tree, which is exactly why Trolio likes it. “It’s a shiny purple tree, after all,” she says of the “pink” one she owns, advising that the shade is much darker and more magenta in person. The tree comes in a rainbow of other hues as well, including white and turquoise. Trolio usually displays her three-foot tinsel tree in her daughters’ room, but thinks the style would be ideal for anyone with “a more kitschy aesthetic.” You can also get it in pre-lit four-foot and seven-foot versions.
